---
title: "Which scale for the violation?"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A violation of the exclusion restriction is a number, *γ*, and a number needs a
unit. In a linear model there is only one: *γ* is the direct effect of the
instrument on the outcome. In a probit there are three natural ones, and apexog
lets you use any of them through `gunits` (R) or `gunits()` (Stata).
Internally the violation always enters the model the same way, as an offset
*z'γ* in the probit index.

## The three scales

**The latent index** (`gunits = "latent"`, the default; synonym `"index"`).
*γ* is a coefficient in the index of the main probit. That probit includes the
control function, and it normalizes the variance of the error *conditional on
the control function* to one. This is the scale of the offset itself, so no
conversion is made. One unit of *γ* moves the probability of the outcome by
roughly the average density of the index, m<sub>φ</sub>, per unit of the
instrument; apexog prints m<sub>φ</sub> in the first "Scale" line.

**Probability points** (`gunits = "pr"`). *γ* is the direct effect of the
instrument on the probability that *y* = 1, per unit of the instrument (0.02
is two percentage points). apexog divides every value you give by m<sub>φ</sub>
from the baseline fit (a variance by m<sub>φ</sub><sup>2</sup>). This is the
scale on which `plausexog` states the violation when it is run on a binary
outcome, as a linear probability model, so it is the scale to use when you
compare the two commands for the same belief. It is also the scale on which
most people find it easiest to say how large a direct effect could plausibly
be.

**The structural latent scale** (`gunits = "structural"`). *γ* is a
coefficient in the structural equation *y\* = x'β + dδ + z'γ + ε* with the
*total* error variance normalized to one, the way latent-variable models are
usually written and simulated. With an endogenous *d*, part of the error is
explained by the control function, so the probit index measures in units of
the smaller conditional standard deviation σ̃ = sd(ε | control function).
apexog estimates σ̃ = (1 + b<sub>cf</sub>' Var(ĉ) b<sub>cf</sub>)<sup>−1/2</sup>
from the baseline fit and divides every value by it; the second "Scale" line
reports it.

<div class="apx-note">

The structural conversion is derived for a **linear first stage**, where the
control function estimates the first-stage error. With a probit, fractional
probit or Poisson first stage it does not apply: in simulations the structural
*γ* enters the index essentially unscaled. Do not combine `gunits = "structural"`
with those first stages; state the violation on the index or in probability
points instead. apexog accepts the combination but prints a warning.

Even with a linear first stage the conversion divides by the baseline σ̃, which
is exact only as *γ* shrinks to zero. With one continuous endogenous regressor
and one instrument, a structural value has a unique index-scale counterpart only below
|π<sub>z</sub>|/σ<sub>v</sub> in absolute value (the first-stage coefficient of
the instrument over the first-stage residual standard deviation). The output
reports that limit (`gs_max`; in Stata `e(gs_max)`) and warns when the range or
the prior draws reach it. The results themselves are not changed.

</div>

## The same belief, three ways

In the example data m<sub>φ</sub> = 0.209 and σ̃ = 0.834. A direct effect of
±0.10 on the latent index is therefore about ±0.0209 in probability and
±0.0834 on the structural scale. Stated in those units, the three calls run
the same grid and give the same bounds:

```{r}
library(apexog)
data(promotion)
f <- promoted ~ tenure + manager
e <- training ~ subsidy

index <- apexog(f, endog = e, data = promotion, gmin = -0.10, gmax = 0.10,
                grid = 5, verbose = FALSE)
m <- index$mphi
s <- index$stilde
c(m_phi = m, sigma_tilde = s)

pr <- apexog(f, endog = e, data = promotion, gunits = "pr",
             gmin = -0.10 * m, gmax = 0.10 * m, grid = 5, verbose = FALSE)
st <- apexog(f, endog = e, data = promotion, gunits = "structural",
             gmin = -0.10 * s, gmax = 0.10 * s, grid = 5, verbose = FALSE)

rbind(index = confint(index), pr = confint(pr), structural = confint(st))
```

The grid stored in the result is always on the latent index; `grid_pr` holds
the exact probability-scale value of each grid point:

```{r}
cbind(index$grid["g_subsidy"], index$grid_pr)
```

## Why the scale matters

The conversions are not cosmetic. If you have a belief on the structural scale
and enter it as if it were on the index, the violation you assume is too small
by the factor σ̃. Under the local-to-zero method the interval is then too
narrow: with a wide prior its coverage approaches 2Φ(*z* σ̃) − 1 instead of the
nominal level (about 0.88 instead of 0.95 at an endogeneity correlation of 0.6
in simulations). Stating the belief in probability points avoids the question
of which latent scale is meant.

## Exact probability scale

The conversion `gunits = "pr"` is a first-order one: it uses m<sub>φ</sub> from
the model with *γ* = 0. apexog also reports, at every refit, the exact
probability-scale value of each instrument's violation in the model refitted
at that violation:

- for a 0/1 instrument, the average change in the probability of the outcome
  when the instrument switches from 0 to 1;
- for any other instrument, the average derivative, mean φ(η)·γ.

The two agree for small violations. They can differ by several percent for a
large violation of a 0/1 instrument when the outcome is close to 0 or 1. With
a linear first stage, as many instruments as endogenous regressors and a
continuous instrument they coincide exactly, as in the example above. The
values are printed beside each range ("exact Pr scale") and stored in
`grid_pr` (UCI) and `sims$gamma_pr` (LTZ); in Stata in `e(grid_pr)` and
`e(gamma_pr_sim)`.

## Both factors describe the baseline fit

m<sub>φ</sub> and σ̃ are computed from the model with *γ* = 0. When the true
violation is not zero that model is misspecified, so both are properties of
that fit rather than structural constants; the conversion is exact as *γ*
shrinks to zero.
